title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement — sliding window, `windowSize - maxFreq ≤ K`.
shortTitle: Longest Repeating Character Replacement — Sliding Window, windowSize - maxFreq ≤ K

s1_definition.profdef: This problem finds the longest substring you can turn into all-identical characters by replacing at most K characters. The sliding-window solution grows a window while the number of characters that would need replacing, the window size minus the count of the most frequent character in it, stays at most K, and shrinks when that budget is exceeded, tracking the maximum valid window. It runs in linear time with constant extra space over a fixed alphabet.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a string of daily status flags and can override at most K of them to make a run of identical flags, to report the longest clean streak achievable. Picture a window over the flags. Inside it, the most common flag is the one you keep; every other flag would have to be overridden. As long as the number of overrides needed is within your budget K, you widen the window. If you would exceed K, you slide the left edge in. You remember the widest window you could legally make uniform.
s1_definition.oneliner: A window is valid when its size minus the most frequent character's count is at most K; grow while valid and track the max.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem finds the longest substring you can turn into all-identical characters by replacing at most K characters. The sliding-window solution grows a window while the number of characters that would need replacing, the window size minus the count of the most frequent character in it, stays at most K, and shrinks when that budget is exceeded, tracking the maximum valid window. It runs in linear time with constant extra space over a fixed alphabet.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has a string of daily status flags and can override at most K of them to make a run of identical flags, to report the longest clean streak achievable. Picture a window over the flags. Inside it, the most common flag is the one you keep; every other flag would have to be overridden. As long as the number of overrides needed is within your budget K, you widen the window. If you would exceed K, you slide the left edge in. You remember the widest window you could legally make uniform.

**One line to remember:** A window is valid when its size minus the most frequent character's count is at most K; grow while valid and track the max.

sections.s2_technical:
The insight is reframing the question. You are not asked which characters to replace, only how long a window can be made uniform with at most K replacements. In any window, the cheapest way to make it uniform is to keep the most frequent character and replace all the others. So the number of replacements needed equals the window size minus the highest character frequency in the window. The window is feasible exactly when that quantity is at most K.

You maintain a window with a left and right index and a frequency count per character, usually an array of twenty-six counts for uppercase letters. You move the right index forward, incrementing the count for the new character, and you keep track of the maximum frequency seen in the window. If the window size, right minus left plus one, minus the maximum frequency exceeds K, the window needs more than K replacements, so you advance the left index, decrementing the count of the character leaving, shrinking the window by one. You update the answer with the current window size whenever it is valid.

A subtle and famous point is that you do not need to recompute the maximum frequency exactly when the window shrinks. You can let the tracked maximum frequency be a high-water mark that never decreases. This is safe because the answer only ever grows when a window larger than the current best is found, and that can only happen when a genuinely higher frequency appears. Keeping a non-decreasing maximum avoids an inner loop to recompute it and preserves linear time. This optimization surprises many people, and explaining why it does not produce a wrong larger answer is a strong senior signal.

Another senior point is why the window never shrinks below the best valid size. Because you only advance the left index by one each time the condition is violated, the window size never decreases overall; it stays the same or grows. So once you have found a window of a certain size, the window width is maintained as a floor, and the maximum you report is monotonic. For a fixed alphabet the frequency array gives constant space; for an open alphabet you use a map.

A small finance-domain example: `int[] cnt=new int[26]; int l=0,maxFreq=0,best=0; for(int r=0;r<s.length();r++){ maxFreq=Math.max(maxFreq, ++cnt[s.charAt(r)-'A']); if((r-l+1)-maxFreq>k){ cnt[s.charAt(l)-'A']--; l++; } best=Math.max(best,r-l+1); }` finds the longest achievable uniform run.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India records a string of daily account status flags, each a single letter, and a feature reports the longest streak that could be made uniform by overriding at most K flags, for example to estimate the best achievable clean-status run after limited corrections. The flag history is long, so the scan must be linear. Longest Repeating Character Replacement is exactly this.

This is exactly how the problem works in Java — a sliding window kept valid by the rule that window size minus the most frequent flag's count stays within the K override budget.

Problem 2 — When K is zero, the answer is just the longest run of identical flags already present, and an empty history gives zero, both of which the same code must handle. This shows the zero-budget and empty-input edge cases alongside the high-water-mark frequency trick.

What the code will do: a `StreakOptimizer` with `longestUniformStreak(String flags, int k)` using the sliding window with a frequency array and a non-decreasing max frequency. The demo reports the best achievable streak for a flag history.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the flag history `AABABBA` with a replacement budget K of one.

Step 1: left is zero, all counts zero, maxFreq zero, best zero. Right at index zero is `A`; its count becomes one, maxFreq becomes one. Window size one minus maxFreq one is zero, which is within K, so best becomes one.

Step 2: right at index one is `A`; count of A becomes two, maxFreq becomes two. Window size two minus two is zero, within K, best becomes two. Right at index two is `B`; count of B becomes one, maxFreq stays two. Window size three minus two is one, within K, best becomes three.

Step 3: right at index three is `A`; count of A becomes three, maxFreq becomes three. Window size four minus three is one, within K, best becomes four. So with one override of the single B, the four-character window AABA can be made uniform.

Step 4: right at index four is `B`; count of B becomes two, maxFreq stays three. Window size five minus three is two, which exceeds K of one, so we shrink: decrement the count of the leftmost A and advance left to one. Window size is now four, and best stays four.

Step 5: the scan continues similarly, always keeping the window size at least four because the window never shrinks below the best found, and maxFreq as a high-water mark avoids recomputation. The final best is four. For K of zero on the same string the window can never override anything, so the answer is the longest existing identical run, which is two for AA, and for ABAB with K of two every character can be overridden so the whole length four is achievable.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T21:10:00Z INFO Longest uniform streak = 4
2026-10-26T21:10:00Z INFO Streak = 4
2026-10-26T21:10:00Z INFO Longest uniform streak = 4
2026-10-26T21:10:00Z INFO Streak = 4
2026-10-26T21:10:00Z INFO Longest uniform streak = 2
2026-10-26T21:10:00Z INFO Streak = 2
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: "AABABBA"  k=1  left=0 maxFreq=0 best=0
    │
    ▼
  for right: count[c]++; maxFreq=max; if (size - maxFreq) > k shrink left
    │ A,A → maxFreq=2 size2 ok best=2
    │ B   → size3-2=1 ok best=3
    │ A   → maxFreq=3 size4-3=1 ok best=4
    │ B   → size5-3=2 > 1 → shrink left=1 (best stays 4)
    ▼
  best = 4   (k=0 → 2 ; "ABAB",k=2 → 4)
    ▼
  Output: longest achievable uniform streak
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Longest Repeating Character Replacement asks for the longest substring that can be made all-identical by replacing at most K characters, and the reframing that unlocks it is that in any window the cheapest way to make it uniform is to keep the most frequent character and replace the rest, so the replacements needed equal the window size minus the highest character frequency. The window is feasible exactly when that quantity is at most K.

I keep a sliding window with a frequency count per character and track the maximum frequency inside it. I expand the right edge, and whenever the window size minus the maximum frequency exceeds K, meaning it would need more than K replacements, I advance the left edge by one to shrink it. I update the answer with the current window size whenever it is valid, in linear time with a constant-size frequency array over a fixed alphabet.

The clever optimization I always explain is that I let the tracked maximum frequency be a high-water mark that never decreases, instead of recomputing it when the window shrinks. This is safe because the best answer only grows when a genuinely larger window appears, which requires a truly higher frequency, so a stale maximum can never inflate the result. Combined with the fact that the window only advances the left edge by one at a time, so the window size never drops below the best found, this keeps the whole scan linear.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on daily account status flag histories to report the longest streak that could be made uniform by overriding at most K flags, estimating the best achievable clean-status run after limited corrections, handling the zero-budget case as the longest existing identical run. Explaining the size-minus-maxFreq validity rule, the non-decreasing maximum trick and why it stays correct, and the monotonic window shows the interviewer that I understand the subtlety that makes this harder than the plain distinct-substring window.
